The Bible opens with God creating "the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). It closes with "a new heaven and a new earth" (Revelation 21:1). Between these two texts, the phrase appears again and again. Sometimes it plainly means the sky and the ground. At other times it seems to carry a second meaning. Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses against Israel. Isaiah says God planted the heavens when he said to Zion, "You are my people." Jeremiah sees the land of Judah return to "formless and empty". Jesus says heaven and earth will pass away, in the same breath as a promise about "this generation". This study asks one main question: when Scripture speaks of heaven and earth passing away and being made new, does it mean the physical universe, the covenant world of Israel centred on the temple, or both? It sets out the covenantal (fulfilled) reading at its strongest. This reading holds that the old-covenant order, with its temple, priests and sacrifices, was a small "heaven and earth" that passed away in AD 70, and that the new heavens and new earth are the new-covenant world in Christ. It also gives the other main readings fairly: the renewal of this creation, its dissolution and replacement, the already/not-yet view, and the full preterist and covenant-creation positions. Along the way it looks at the tabernacle as a small model of the cosmos (Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.7; Jewish War 5.5.4-5), creation words that return when God forms, judges or renews his people, key Hebrew and Greek words, and Isaiah 65-66 beside Revelation 21-22. Every view here is held by Christians who love Scripture. The aim is to understand each one well, not to win an argument.
Renewal of this creation
God will not throw away the world he made. At Christ's return he will free it from decay and make it new, the way he will raise our bodies. The new earth is this earth, healed and glorified.
The new heavens and new earth are this same cosmos renewed, set free from the curse at the resurrection of the body.
Irenaeus; John Calvin; Abraham Kuyper; Herman Bavinck; Anthony Hoekema; Albert Wolters; N. T. Wright; J. Richard Middleton; many Reformed, Catholic and Orthodox teachers.

It fits Romans 8, where creation itself waits to be freed, and Acts 3:21, which speaks of the restoring of all things. It keeps a close link between the resurrection of the body and the renewal of the world: Jesus' body was the same body, changed. It honours God's verdict that creation is good (Genesis 1:31). Early manuscripts of 2 Peter 3:10 read "will be found" or "laid bare", which suggests purging, not erasing.

Texts such as 2 Peter 3:10-12, Isaiah 51:6 and Revelation 20:11 use strong language of passing, melting and fleeing, which a renewal reading must soften. It usually treats Matthew 24:35 as a proverb about the stability of Jesus' words, which some find weak beside verse 34. Covenantal readers say it overlooks how often "heaven and earth" language is used for Israel's covenant order.
Dissolution and replacement

The present universe will be burned up and pass out of existence. God will then create a brand-new heaven and earth. 2 Peter 3:10 is read literally: the elements are the physical building blocks of matter.
The physical heavens and earth will be destroyed by fire, and God will create a wholly new universe in their place.

Lutheran orthodoxy (Johann Gerhard; later Francis Pieper) spoke of the annihilation of the world's substance; many dispensational writers such as John Walvoord and J. Dwight Pentecost; many popular Bible teachers.

It takes the strong words of 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 20:11 ("earth and heaven fled away") at face value. Psalms 102:25-26 and Hebrews 1:10-12 contrast the perishing creation with the unchanging Lord. It stresses that the new world is God's gift, not a human achievement.

It sits uneasily with Romans 8:21, where creation itself is set free, not destroyed. The flood comparison in 2 Peter 3:6 involves a world that "perished" yet was not annihilated. The best manuscripts of 2 Peter 3:10 end with "will be found", not "burned up". It also struggles with texts that say the earth stands for ever (Psalms 104:5; Ecclesiastes 1:4).
Covenantal reading of the passing texts, with a future resurrection

Several "passing" texts describe the end of the old-covenant order in AD 70. This includes Matthew 24:35, Hebrews 12:26-28 and, for some, 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 21. But Christ's bodily return, the resurrection of the dead and the final judgment are still future.
"Heaven and earth" in key prophecies is covenant language for the temple-centred world of Israel, which passed in AD 70; the final resurrection is still to come.

Some partial preterists. John Lightfoot (1602-1675) read Matthew 24:29-35 of Jerusalem's fall. John Owen (1616-1683) read 2 Peter 3:5-13 and Hebrews 12:26-27 as including the end of the Jewish church-state. John Brown of Edinburgh read Matthew 5:18 this way. Modern writers such as James Jordan and Peter Leithart. Others in this camp, such as J. Marcellus Kik and Kenneth Gentry, read Matthew 24:35 or 2 Peter 3 of the final end.

It takes the time words seriously: "this generation" (Matthew 24:34), "ready to vanish" (Hebrews 8:13), "yet once more" (Hebrews 12:26). It uses the prophets' own language of cosmic collapse for the fall of nations (Isaiah 13:10; Ezekiel 32:7). It has respected older Protestant voices. It keeps the creeds' future hope.

Critics say it can blur when a text means the old covenant and when it means the cosmos, and partial preterists disagree among themselves about which texts belong where. Revelation 21:4 promises no more death, which seems beyond AD 70. Some argue that 2 Peter 3:5-7 compares the coming fire with a real flood on the physical world.
Full preterist covenant-world reading

All end-time prophecy, including the coming of Christ, the resurrection and the new heavens and new earth, was fulfilled in the events that closed with AD 70. The new Jerusalem of Revelation 21 is the church in the new covenant now.
The first heaven and earth of Revelation 21:1 is the old-covenant world; it passed in AD 70, and the new creation is the present new-covenant age in its fullness.
J. Stuart Russell (The Parousia, 1878) is often seen as the classic statement; Max R. King; Don K. Preston; others in the modern preterist movement.

It is very consistent with the time texts of Revelation ("soon", "near", Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:10). It reads Revelation 21 in line with Isaiah 65, where death and sinners still exist (Isaiah 65:20). It explains why the bride, the city and the holy mountain are pictures of a people (Revelation 21:9-10).

It sets aside the future bodily resurrection and final judgment that all the historic creeds confess. Most Christians, including most partial preterists, see it as outside historic orthodoxy. Critics point to 1 Corinthians 15:42-54, 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 and the warning against those who said the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18). The ongoing reality of death seems hard to square with Revelation 21:4.
Covenant-creation reading of Genesis 1

This reading goes further. It says Genesis 1 itself is not mainly about the making of the physical universe. It describes God forming his covenant people, the first "heavens and earth" that later passed away. This is a minority view even among full preterists, and many of them reject it.
The "heavens and earth" of Genesis 1:1 are the covenant world God began with Adam, so the passing of the "first heaven and earth" (Revelation 21:1) completes the story that Genesis 1 began.

A small group within full preterism, set out at length by Timothy Martin and Jeffrey Vaughn (Beyond Creation Science, 2007). Most preterists, partial and full, do not hold it. Almost no other Christian tradition does.

It notices real links: Jeremiah 4:23 uses Genesis 1:2 words for Judah's ruin, and Isaiah 51:16 uses creation words for Israel's founding. It reads the Bible as one covenant story from first page to last. Its defenders say it frees Genesis from being forced into modern science debates.

Genesis 1 names plants, sea creatures, birds, cattle and the lights in the sky, which read as the physical world. Other texts look back to Genesis 1 as the making of all things: Exodus 20:11, Psalms 104, Acts 14:15, Romans 1:20, and Jesus in Mark 10:6. Key word arguments (such as "host" in Genesis 2:1 meaning a mass of people) are not supported by most Hebrew scholars. It cuts the covenant from the created world rather than placing it within it.
Inaugurated new creation: already and not yet

The new creation has already begun in the risen Christ and in all who are joined to him. Yet the full renewal of the cosmos waits for his return. The old-covenant order ended with the cross and AD 70, but the new heavens and earth will be complete only at the resurrection.
New creation is present now in Christ and his people, and will be completed in a renewed cosmos at his coming.
G. K. Beale (A New Testament Biblical Theology, 2011); Geerhardus Vos; Herman Ridderbos; Anthony Hoekema; Douglas Moo; many amillennial and postmillennial teachers.

It explains why Paul can say the new creation is here (2 Corinthians 5:17) while creation still groans (Romans 8:22). It matches the pattern of Christ's resurrection as the "firstfruits" of a later harvest (1 Corinthians 15:23). It can accept much of the covenantal reading of the temple while keeping the cosmic hope.

Preterist readers say it delays texts that carry near time words. Some replacement readers say it makes the new earth too much like the present one. Its users do not always agree where a given text sits on the "already" or "not yet" side.
What did Jesus mean by "heaven and earth will pass away"?

Matthew 24:34-35 and its parallels set a time limit and speak of heaven and earth passing. These questions ask whether Jesus meant the cosmos, the temple order, or simply that his words outlast all things.
Was the temple a small heaven and earth?
Josephus and later readers saw the tabernacle and temple as a model of the cosmos. These questions look at that idea and what it means when the temple falls.
Can "heaven and earth" stand for a people?

Moses speaks to the heavens and earth as witnesses. Abraham's seed is like the stars and the dust. Joseph's dream uses sun, moon and stars for a family. These questions test how far this picture language goes.
How do the Psalms use heaven and earth?
The Psalms call the heavens to praise, to declare, to witness and to perish like a garment. These questions ask when the words mean sky and ground and when they point to God's people.
Why do the prophets shake the heavens?
Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel and Haggai use darkened suns and shaken heavens for judgment on nations and on Israel. These questions look at that language and its use in the New Testament.
What passes away in 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 21?
2 Peter 3 speaks of fire and melting elements; Revelation 21 of a first heaven and earth that passed away. These questions weigh the covenantal and the cosmic readings.
What are the new heavens and the new earth?
Isaiah 65-66 and Revelation 21-22 describe a new world, a new Jerusalem and a people of joy. These questions ask whether this is the church now, the renewed cosmos later, or both.
How should we decide, and why does it matter?
These questions deal with method: Scripture and tradition, the creeds, literal and figurative reading, and what difference each view makes for faith and life.
Did Jesus mean that the physical universe would vanish within one generation?
On the fulfilled reading, no. Jesus tied the passing of "heaven and earth" to his own generation, so he must have meant the old covenant world centred on the temple, not the stars and the planet.

In Matthew 24:34-35 Jesus says two things side by side. First, "this generation" will not pass until all these things happen. Second, heaven and earth will pass, but his words will not. If "heaven and earth" meant the physical cosmos, the prophecy failed, because the sky and the ground are still here. Read covenantally, the saying fits its setting. Jesus had just left the temple and said that not one stone would stay on another (Matthew 24:1-2). The disciples asked when this would happen. The answer ends with a pledge: the old order will go, but my word stands. In AD 70 the temple, the priesthood and the sacrifices ended. On this reading, that was the "heaven and earth" that passed, and it passed inside the forty years Jesus gave.
Jesus spoke about AD 30. The temple burned in August AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-8), about forty years later, the length of one biblical generation.
Mark 13:30-31 and Luke 21:32-33 repeat the same two sayings together, so the link between "this generation" and "heaven and earth" is in all three Gospels.

Many futurists and amillennialists say verse 35 is a proverb: even if the universe passed away, Christ's words would not. Others, including some partial preterists, see verse 35 as a turn toward the final end of the present cosmos at the second coming, with verse 34 limited to AD 70.
Does Scripture say the earth will remain forever?

Yes. Several texts say God founded the earth so that it stands forever. The fulfilled reading uses this to argue that the "heaven and earth" which passes away must be something other than the physical planet.

Psalms 104:5 says God set the earth on its foundations so that it will never be moved. Ecclesiastes 1:4 says generations come and go, but the earth stays forever. Psalms 78:69 says God built his sanctuary like the high heavens, like the earth he founded forever. On the fulfilled reading, Scripture does not contradict itself. If the physical earth abides, then texts about heaven and earth "passing away" must use the phrase in a covenant sense. Psalms 78:69 even compares the temple to heaven and earth. That supports the idea that the temple world could be called "heaven and earth". When that sanctuary fell, a covenant "heaven and earth" ended, while the physical earth went on.
Psalms 78:69 likens the Jerusalem sanctuary to the heights and to the earth. The temple was built to mirror the cosmos.
Ecclesiastes 1:4 contrasts passing human generations with the earth that stays. The point is the earth's lasting, not its end.

Other readers note that the Hebrew word olam can mean "for a very long age" rather than "without end". They say these texts praise the earth's stability under God, and do not rule out a final renewal of creation (Romans 8:21; 2 Peter 3:13). Many hold that the earth is renewed, not destroyed, so it still "remains".
If the physical cosmos did not pass away, what "heaven and earth" did pass away in that generation?
On the covenantal reading, it was the old covenant order: the temple, its priesthood and sacrifices, and the nation built around them. That world ended when Rome destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.

Jesus spoke these words while predicting the fall of the temple (Matthew 24:1-2). The prophets often used "heaven and earth" for a people and its ruling order. Isaiah spoke of God planting the heavens and founding the earth when he said to Zion, "You are my people" (Isaiah 51:16). Jeremiah described Judah's ruin as the earth returning to "formless and empty" (Jeremiah 4:23). Hebrews, written while the temple still stood, said the first covenant was old and "ready to vanish away" (Hebrews 8:13). On the fulfilled reading, these lines meet in AD 70. The temple, the centre of Israel's world, was burned. Sacrifice stopped. The old covenant structure passed, and the new covenant order in Christ stood alone.
Hebrews 8:13: the first covenant was "growing old" and near to vanishing. The writer spoke as if the end was close.
Josephus reports that the temple was burned on the same day of the year that Babylon had burned the first temple (Jewish War 6.4.5).

Futurists and most amillennialists answer that no "heaven and earth" has yet passed; Jesus was speaking of the final end. Partial preterists who divide the chapter say AD 70 fulfilled verses 1-34, but verse 35 looks to the end of the present cosmos. All agree AD 70 ended the temple system.
Did the disciples ask about the end of the world or the end of the age (Matthew 24:3)?
They asked about the end of the "age" (Greek aion), after Jesus foretold the temple's fall. The fulfilled reading says they meant the end of the old covenant age, not the end of the physical world.

Jesus had just said that Jerusalem's house would be left desolate (Matthew 23:38) and that the temple stones would be thrown down (24:2). The disciples asked three things: when this will happen, what sign will show his coming, and what will mark the end of the age (24:3). The Greek word is aion, "age", not kosmos, "world". Older English Bibles said "end of the world", which led many readers to think of the planet. On the fulfilled reading, a Jew in AD 30 linked the fall of the temple with the close of an era. Jesus did not correct their question. He answered it, and placed it within "this generation" (24:34).
The KJV says "end of the world"; most modern versions say "end of the age", which follows the Greek aion.
Hebrews 9:26 uses the same phrase in the plural: Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" to put away sin. That was in the first century.

Futurist and many amillennial readers agree the word is "age", but they say "this age" runs until Christ's return (Matthew 13:39-40; 28:20). They hold that the disciples blended the temple's fall with the final end, and Jesus answered both, which is why his reply looks near and far.
What do "the end of the age" and "the age to come" mean?
On the fulfilled reading, "this age" was the age of the Mosaic covenant and "the age to come" was the messianic age of the new covenant. The changeover came between the cross and AD 70.

Paul told the Corinthians that "the ends of the ages" had come upon them (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews says Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" (Hebrews 9:26). Peter called his own time "these last times" (1 Peter 1:20) and said "the end of all things is at hand" (1 Peter 4:7). Jewish teachers spoke of "this age" and "the age to come", meaning the time before and after the Messiah. Jesus used the same pair in Matthew 12:32. On the fulfilled reading, the old age closed when the temple and its sacrifices ended. The age to come is the Christian era, where the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience (Hebrews 9:14). Older scholars such as Milton Terry read Matthew 24:3 in this way.
1 Corinthians 10:11, written about AD 55, says the ends of the ages had reached Paul's readers.
Matthew 12:32 speaks of forgiveness "neither in this age nor in the age to come", the common Jewish two-age pattern.

Many scholars, including amillennialists and dispensationalists, hold that the "age to come" fully begins at Christ's return and the resurrection (Luke 20:34-36). They speak of an "already and not yet": the new age broke in with Christ, but the present evil age continues until the end (Galatians 1:4).
Does Jesus change the subject at Matthew 24:35-36?
The fulfilled reading in this chapter says no. Verse 35 sums up the darkened sun and falling stars of verse 29, and verse 36 speaks of the exact day of that same judgment, which only the Father knew.

Some respected partial preterists, such as J. Marcellus Kik and Kenneth Gentry, hold that verses 1-34 describe AD 70 and that verse 36 moves to the final coming. Charles Spurgeon also saw a change at verse 36. The fulfilled reading in this chapter disagrees. Verse 35 does not start a new topic. It confirms what Jesus has just said. Verse 29 used the old prophetic picture of a falling sky. Verse 35 says the same thing in plain words: heaven and earth will pass. Verse 36 then adds that the day and hour are unknown. The disciples had asked "when" (24:3). Jesus gave the generation (24:34), but not the day. John Gill and John Lightfoot both read verse 36 as the day of Jerusalem's fall.
Jesus told them to pray that their flight would not be in winter or on a Sabbath (Matthew 24:20). This shows that the exact season was unknown even inside the generation.
Adam Clarke noted that the Greek hora can mean "season" and tied verse 36 to the siege of Jerusalem.

Those who see a change point to "but of that day" (Greek peri de), which often marks a new topic (1 Corinthians 7:1). They note that signs are given before verse 34 but none after, and that the later parables stress delay. They read verses 36-25:46 as the final return.
Are the darkened sun and falling stars of Matthew 24:29 another way to say "heaven and earth will pass away"?
On the fulfilled reading, yes. The prophets used a collapsing sky to describe the fall of a nation and its rulers. Verse 29 uses that language for Jerusalem, and verse 35 says it again plainly.

Jesus quotes the prophets in verse 29. Isaiah 13:10 used the darkened sun, moon and stars for the fall of Babylon. Isaiah 34:4 used the rolling up of the sky for the judgment of Edom. In Scripture, when stars fall to earth, it pictures rulers brought low (Isaiah 14:12; Daniel 8:10). On the fulfilled reading, Jesus uses the same picture for the end of Israel's ruling order. Verse 29 says it happens "immediately after the tribulation of those days". Verse 34 says it happens in this generation. So the sky falling in verse 29 and heaven and earth passing in verse 35 describe one event: the end of the old covenant world of the temple, upheld by the leaders who "crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8).
Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC. The stars did not literally fall, yet Isaiah 13:10 used that picture for it.
Daniel 8:10 shows a horn throwing some stars to the ground. Daniel 8:24 explains them as "the holy people".

Most futurists take verse 29 as real cosmic signs before Christ's return (Luke 21:25-26). Many amillennialists see both a near and a final meaning. Even many who accept the prophetic imagery still say verse 35, unlike verse 29, contrasts lasting words with a literally passing cosmos.
Does "this generation" (24:34) versus "that day" (24:36) prove that two different events are meant?
The fulfilled reading says no. "That" is the natural word for any future point, near or far. "That day" can be the still-future day within "this generation" when Jerusalem would fall.

Some argue that if Jesus meant the same event, he would have said "this day". But "this" points to something present and "that" points to something farther off. The standard Greek lexicon of Arndt and Gingrich notes the same sense for houtos (this) and ekeinos (that). The generation was present when Jesus spoke. The day of judgment was still future, so it was "that day". Prophets often called a coming judgment "that day" when it was near. On the fulfilled reading, "that day" is the day the Son of Man came against Jerusalem, a day still ahead for the disciples, but inside their lifetime.
Isaiah 2:12-20 and Zephaniah 1:7-15 call coming judgments on Judah "that day"; those came on Judah in history.
Luke 17:31 says "in that day" about fleeing from the housetop, a warning tied to the war on Jerusalem.

Partial preterists such as Kenneth Gentry argue the shift from "this" to "that" is a deliberate contrast between near and far. Futurists add that Jesus said even he did not know the day, which they think fits a distant final coming better than an event he had just placed within a generation.
Why does Jesus give no signs after Matthew 24:36?
On the fulfilled reading, the signs had already been given in verses 4-34. After that, Jesus moves from signs to a call for watchfulness, because the exact day would still come by surprise.

Some say that verses 1-34 have many signs, but verses 36-51 have none, so a different, sign-less event must be meant. The fulfilled reading offers two answers. First, all the signs needed to know the general time were already listed: false messiahs, wars, persecution, the gospel preached, and armies around Jerusalem (Luke 21:20). Second, the teaching changes from "what to look for" to "how to live while you wait". A person can know a season and still not know the hour. Jesus says this himself: when you see the fig tree put out leaves, you know summer is near (Matthew 24:32-33). Yet the master still comes at an hour the servant does not expect (24:44).
Luke 21:20-21: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, flee. This was a clear sign. Christians fled to Pella before the siege (Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3).
A farmer knows harvest is near from the crops, but not the day the storm will come.

Readers who see two events say the contrast is real: an event with signs (AD 70) and an event with no warning (the final return, 1 Thessalonians 5:2-3). They argue that saying "no one knows the day" right after giving a generation shows the second event has no date limit.
Do the plural "those days" and the singular "that day" point to two different events?
The fulfilled reading says no. The "days" are the time of tribulation before the end. The "day" is the single day when judgment fell. Both belong to the same generation, as with Noah.

Some argue that the many "days" of the great tribulation (Matthew 24:22) belong to AD 70, but the one "day" (24:36) must be the second coming, which happens in a moment. The fulfilled reading answers that verse 29 says the sky falls "immediately after the tribulation of those days". So the days lead up to a day. Jesus himself uses this pattern with Noah: "the days before the flood" and "the day Noah entered the ark" (24:38). The same people lived through both the days and the day. In the same way, the generation lived through the tribulation and then the day when the city and sanctuary fell.
Noah's neighbours lived through the "days" of warning and then the one "day" the flood came (Genesis 7:11-13).
The siege of Jerusalem lasted months (spring to September AD 70), but the temple burned on a single day (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5).

Kenneth Gentry and others say the contrast is meaningful: the long tribulation versus a sudden coming "in the twinkling of an eye" (1 Corinthians 15:52). Futurists agree and place the singular day at the end of history.
What does "as in the days of Noah" teach: great wickedness or ordinary life?
Jesus stresses ordinary life: eating, drinking and marrying. People carried on as usual and did not expect judgment. The point is surprise, not a list of special sins.

Some popular teachers have said "marrying and giving in marriage" means sexual sin or wife-swapping. The text does not say that. Marrying is normal (Matthew 22:30). Luke adds the days of Lot: people bought, sold, planted and built (Luke 17:28). These are everyday tasks. D. A. Carson notes that Jesus makes no direct mention of the sin of that generation here. Noah's age was wicked (Genesis 6:5), but the point of the comparison is that life looked normal. On the fulfilled reading, Jerusalem in the 60s AD was the same. Life went on, and many ignored the warning until the armies came. Peter speaks of mockers who say all things continue as they were (2 Peter 3:3-4).
Noah was warned about "things not yet seen" (Hebrews 11:7). His neighbours saw no sign in the sky.
Luke 17:28-29 lists buying, selling, planting and building in Sodom: daily business, not crimes.

Most interpreters of every school agree that the stress is on normal life and surprise. Some dispensational writers add that the end-time world will also be morally corrupt, as in Noah's day, and read Luke's list as showing a careless, godless culture.
Are those "taken" in Matthew 24:40-41 taken in a rapture or taken in judgment?
In context, they are taken in judgment. The flood "took them all away", and Luke says it "destroyed them all". Noah was the one left to carry on.

Jesus links the two people in the field to the flood: it came and "took them all away" (Matthew 24:39). Luke states the same fact as "destroyed them all" (Luke 17:27, 29). So "taken" means taken by judgment. Noah and his family were the ones left. When the disciples asked "Where, Lord?", Jesus answered that where the body is, the vultures gather (Luke 17:37). That points to death, not rescue. Even the dispensational scholar John Walvoord wrote that in this passage the one taken is taken in judgment. On the fulfilled reading, this fits Judea in AD 66-70, when many were killed or carried off by Roman soldiers, while those who fled survived.
